               A2 SEGMENT AFFECTED LANDOWNERS COALITION'S
                            INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF


TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:


I. REQUESTED RELIEF AND SUMMARY OF POSITION

The A2 Segment Affected Landowners Coalition opposes the project and requests that

the application be denied or deferred. At minimum, the record does not show that less

intrusive alternatives were fully evaluated before the Applicants proposed a new 765-kV

greenfield transmission line across private rural land.

If the Commission approves the project, it should not approve any route using Segment

A2. A2 is not required to leave the Bell County East Switch area, not required by the

filed route set, and not justified by the record. Every principal route discussed at


                                         A2 SEGMENT AFFECTED LANDOWNERS COALITION'S
                                                                INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF
                                                                       PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                                SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                 Page 1 of 27
 hearing, including Routes 487, 296, 894, and 392, uses A2, but repeated use is not

proof of necessity. The filed route set includes reasonable non-A2 alternatives, including

Route 1245 and other reasonable filed alternatives such as Routes 659, 705, 706, and

836. [Applicants Ex. 23, Combined Data Table.]

A2 would place a new 765-kV corridor through an established rural residential and

agricultural community that has already absorbed substantial energy infrastructure. The

record shows reliance on rural residential character and land-use restrictions, not

consent to become an energy corridor. A2 would also remove existing solar generation,

burden Highway 190 frontage, and cross a corridor with documented ponds, stock

tanks, creeks, drainage features, and livestock-water resources.

The route tables do not fully capture those impacts. PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC §

25.101 require more than a mechanical route-table comparison. They require

consideration of need, community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental

integrity, cost, land use, landowner impacts, and prudent avoidance. Because

reasonable filed non-A2 alternatives remain available, the impacts of A2 are avoidable

and should not be imposed.


II. THE PROJECT SHOULD BE DENIED OR DEFERRED UNTIL REASONABLE

ALTERNATIVES ARE FULLY EVALUATED

The Coalition opposes the project itself, not only Segment A2. The record supports a

narrower point. Applicants presented a transmission solution based largely on ERCOT
                                        A2 SEGMENT AFFECTED LANDOWNERS COALITION'S
                                                              INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF
                                                                     PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                              SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
                                                                               Page 2 of 27
 import-path modeling, but the record does not show that generation-side, load-side,

existing-corridor, or hybrid alternatives were fully evaluated and rejected in this docket.

Applicants’ own witnesses framed the problem as a “localized generation deficit,”

meaning insufficient generation near the load being served. Mr. Gurley also agreed that

765-kV lines are useful for moving large amounts of power over long distances and from

one ERCOT region to another. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 217:6-218:11.] He further testified that

ERCOT selected the endpoints because they were efficient hubs for taking power from

other parts of the system and using the 765-kV line to transport that power to West

Texas. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 48:8-13.]

That testimony does not prove that local generation would eliminate the project.

Applicants disputed that point. But it does show that the need case depends on

assumptions about load growth, generation location, import capacity, and ERCOT

modeling. No ERCOT witness appeared to defend that modeling. Mr. Gurley confirmed

that ERCOT performed the reliability studies and developed the cost, transfer-capacity,

and loss figures relied on by Applicants, and that Applicants did not independently

calculate those figures. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 49:4-50:10.]

The record also confirms the limits of Applicants’ proof. A 765-kV transmission line does

not generate power. [Tr. Vol. 2 at 120:1-7.] When asked whether Applicants compared

the cost of this import path against local generation in West Texas, Mr. Martin

answered, “We don’t build generation.” [Tr. Vol. 4 at 42:23-43:2.] He then confirmed that


                                         A2 SEGMENT AFFECTED LANDOWNERS COALITION'S
                                                                INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF
                                                                      PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                               SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
                                                                                  Page 3 of 27
 generation is generally handled by the private sector and that Applicants work with

generators through the interconnection process. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 43:3-12.] That answer is

understandable for transmission utilities, but it also shows why this record should not be

treated as a full comparison of transmission, generation, load-side, and hybrid

alternatives.

The record further shows that some existing corridor alternatives were not studied. Mr.

Marusak testified that Oncor and LCRA did not evaluate routing along the southern

existing transmission-line corridor from Lampasas to Big Hill East. He also

acknowledged that routes not paralleling existing transmission corridors create

additional impacts. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 140:1-143:20.]

For those reasons, the Commission should deny or defer the application until the need,

scope, cost, and reasonable alternatives are more fully evaluated. If the Commission

approves the project, it should not compound the record gap by selecting a route using

Segment A2 when reasonable filed non-A2 alternatives remain available.


III. A2 IS NOT REQUIRED BY THE EASTERN OPENING

The Coalition’s focus on Segment A2 has been consistent and reasonable. Coalition

members are self-represented landowners who live along and near A2, and the first

meaningful routing decision affecting them occurs immediately after the shared eastern

opening. Every proposed route begins at Bell County East Switch with Links A0 and A1.


                                         A2 SEGMENT AFFECTED LANDOWNERS COALITION'S
                                                              INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF
                                                                     PUC Docket No. 59475
                                                              SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349
                                                                               Page 4 of 27
 After A1, the available eastern alternatives are A2, A3, and A42. [Applicants Ex. 1, App.

D, Routes of Interest Map, Attachment A.]

Joe and Michelle Burnett testified that 942 of the 1,246 route IDs include Segment A2,

while only 217 include Segment A3. [Joe and Michelle Burnett Ex. 4 at 8.] The principal

hearing routes addressed by the Coalition, including Routes 487, 296, 894, and 392,

use A2. None uses A3 or A42. That explains why Coalition members focused on the A2

versus A3 decision instead of attempting to evaluate every complete route across

multiple counties. Their position has not changed. The complete routes identified in this

brief simply show that the same position can be carried through the filed route set.

The Commission is not bound by the Applicants’ preferred route or any particular route

package. Chairman Smitherman testified that the Commission considers the totality of

the information before it, that the Applicants’ preferred route does not bind the

Commission, and that the Commission often selects a different route. [Tr. Vol. 5 at

196:13-197:8.] Staff witness John Poole likewise confirmed that no mathematical

formula identifies Route 487 as the preferred route and that neither the Applicants nor

the Commission used a mathematical scoring method to select a route. [Tr. Vol. 4 at

87:8-19; Tr. Vol. 4 at 239:22-240:10.] The question is therefore whether reasonable filed

routes exist that avoid A2. The record shows that they do.

It supports the A3/A6/C1 opening instead of the A2/B1/C2 opening used by Route 296

because that substitution avoids A2 and then rejoins the same general Route 296 path

at D11. [Applicants Ex. 23, Combined Data Table, Routes 296 and 705.] This is also

links appear to follow or parallel existing transmission corridors and utility infrastructure

to a greater extent than A2 and create less impact to occupied residences and rural

residential communities. [Brandon Fortie Direct Testimony, Interchange Item 4807 at

6:3-10.]

The engineering evidence also weighs against defaulting to A2. A2 introduces a 90-

degree turn at A1 that A3 does not. Ms. Cooley testified that turning locations increase

cost, that a 90-degree turn requires a full-tension dead-end structure, and that dead-end

structures require more steel than tangent structures. [Tr. Vol. 2 at 121:1-17; Tr. Vol. 2

at 195:22-196:7; Tr. Vol. 4 at 58:23-60:4.] Staff witness Poole likewise agreed that

turning structures are a significant cost variable and that route cost estimates do not

separately identify routes requiring additional dead-end structures. [Tr. Vol. 4 at 208:1-

20.]

These routes are not presented as equal recommendations. Route 1245 is the

Coalition’s strongest overall non-A2 recommendation. Route 705 is the cleanest proof

that the A3 opening can replace Route 296’s A2 opening. Route 659 is the practical

non-A2 comparison to Route 894. Route 836 is the closest non-A2 comparison to Route

487. Route 706 is a backup to Route 705. Taken together, the filed route data and

engineering testimony show that A2 is not necessary, not merely that another route

exists somewhere in the filed route set.

 A. A2 Creates a Specific and Avoidable Solar-Generation Conflict

A2 creates a hard, measurable impact that the route table does not capture. The

Environmental Assessment states that solar farms are common and expansive near

Bell County East Switch, and Mr. Marusak agreed that remains true. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 237:8-

238:3.] During cross-examination, Joe Burnett established that a 1,400-foot crossing

through a 200-foot right-of-way would remove more than six acres of existing solar

generation, and Mr. Marusak agreed with that calculation. Applicants also

acknowledged that they had not calculated the generating capacity that would be

permanently removed if Link A2 were constructed. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 238:9-239:5.]

That is not a generalized landowner concern. It is a known, quantifiable, and avoidable

impact. Mr. Marusak testified that A3 was routed around the solar facilities and was

modified after public meetings to increase distance from habitable structures and

address landowner concerns. [Tr. Vol. 3 at 239:6-240:4.] A2 would remove more than

six acres of existing solar facilities, and Applicants did not calculate the generating

capacity that would be lost. That comparison weighs strongly against selecting A2.

testimony regarding a planned mixed-animal veterinary clinic on family Highway 190

property. That is different from a vague future homesite claim. Highway frontage has

followed by cumulative utility buildout around established homes and planned

homesites.

residential character of the area, and that they chose and built there because they were

For the reasons stated, the A2 Segment Affected Landowners Coalition respectfully

Commission's routing criteria.
